'''Kihisatsumi''' ({{lang|ja|岐比佐都美}}; also {{lang|ja|来日羅積}}{{Sfn|高嶋|1995a|pp=144-151}}) is a figure who appears in the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|lt=Kojiki|lt_ja=古事記}}''.

== Overview ==
Kihisatsumi appears in the section on {{ill|Emperor Suinin|ja|垂仁天皇|lt=Emperor Suinin|lt_ja=垂仁天皇}} in the middle book of the ''Kojiki''. The figure is not found in the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|lt=Nihon Shoki|lt_ja=日本書紀}}'', the ''{{ill|Shinsen Shōjiroku|ja|新撰姓氏録|lt=Shinsen Shōjiroku|lt_ja=新撰姓氏録}}'' or similar works.{{Sfn|島根県古代文化センター|2014|p=149}} Kihisatsumi is held to be the ancestor of the Izumo ''kuni no miyatsuko''.

== Account ==
=== Kojiki ===
By {{ill|Futomani|ja|太占|lt=futomani divination|lt_ja=太占}} it was found that the reason why Emperor Suinin's son {{ill|Homutsuwake|ja|誉津別命|lt=Homuchiwake|lt_ja=本牟智和気御子}} could not speak was a curse from the will of the {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主|lt=Great God of Izumo|lt_ja=出雲大神}}. The prince travelled to {{ill|Izumo Province|ja|出雲国|lt=Izumo|lt_ja=出雲}} to worship the god, taking {{ill|Akebotatsu no Ōkimi|ja|曙立王|lt=Akebotatsu no Ōkimi|lt_ja=曙立王}} and {{ill|Unakami no Ōkimi|ja|菟上王|lt=Unakami no Ōkimi|lt_ja=菟上王}} with him. When, having worshipped the god, he was about to return to the capital, a bridge of logs with the black bark left on was built across the {{ill|Hii River|ja|斐伊川|lt=Hi River|lt_ja=肥河}}, a temporary palace was put up, and the prince was invited there. Kihisatsumi, ancestor of the Izumo ''kuni no miyatsuko'', decorated a "green-leafed mountain" downstream and was about to offer the great meal (''ōmike''), when the prince spoke and asked: "That thing like a green-leafed mountain downriver looks like a mountain but is not one. Could it be the ritual ground of the {{ill|Hafuri|ja|祝 (神職)|lt=hafuri|lt_ja=祝}} priests who serve {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主|lt=the great god Ashihara-shikoo|lt_ja=葦原色許男大神}} at the Sono-no-miya of Iwakuma in Izumo?" The princes who had been sent with him rejoiced at hearing and seeing this. The prince was lodged at the Nagaho palace of {{ill|Livistona chinensis|ja|ビロウ|lt=ajimasa palms|lt_ja=檳榔}}, and a fast messenger was sent to the emperor.{{Sfn|中村|2009|pp=126-128, 346-348}}

== Interpretation ==
''Kihisa'' is read as an old place name for the area around Mount Butsukyō (identified with the {{ill|Kannabi|ja|神奈備|lt=Kamunabi-yama|lt_ja=神名火山}}), from the Kihisa shrine recorded under {{ill|Izumo District, Shimane|ja|出雲郡|lt=Izumo District|lt_ja=出雲郡}} in the ''{{ill|Izumo no Kuni Fudoki|ja|出雲国風土記|lt=Izumo no Kuni Fudoki|lt_ja=出雲国風土記}}'';{{Sfn|高嶋|1995a|pp=144-151}}{{Sfn|加藤|1978|pp=86-93}}{{Sfn|三谷|1974|pp=471-474}} ''tsu'' is the attributive particle, and ''mi'' is a word for a spirit or divine spirit ({{ill|Spirit|ja|精霊|lt=spirit|lt_ja=精霊}}, {{ill|Soul|ja|霊魂|lt=divine spirit|lt_ja=神霊}}).{{Sfn|高嶋|1995a|pp=144-151}}{{Sfn|加藤|1978|pp=86-93}} Since both names begin with ''Kihisa'', a link has been considered with {{ill|Kihisakamitakahiko|ja|キヒサカミタカヒコ|lt=Kihisakamitakahiko|lt_ja=キヒサカミタカヒコ}} (伎比佐加美高日子命, 天津枳比佐可美高日子命), who appears in the Izumo District section of the ''Izumo no Kuni Fudoki''. One view holds that the two are the same deity;{{Sfn|高嶋|1995a|pp=144-151}} another that a shared origin of the name developed into two different forms, a human and a {{ill|Kami|ja|神 (神道)|lt=god|lt_ja=神}}.{{Sfn|松本|2007|p=231}} Through this link with the god Kihisatsumi is taken to be male,{{Sfn|アンダソヴァ|2012|pp=3-5}} while another view sees Kihisatsumi as a {{ill|Miko|ja|巫女|lt=shamaness|lt_ja=巫女}} who bears the power of water and serves gods and nobles, a "woman of the water".{{Sfn|尾崎|1966|pp=391-392}}

{{ill|Ame-no-Hohi|ja|アメノホヒ|lt=Ame-no-Hohi|lt_ja=アメノホヒ}} is also recorded as an ancestor of the Izumo ''kuni no miyatsuko''. On this point one theory holds that Ame-no-Hohi was a newly created ancestral god with no original connection to Izumo, linked to the Izumo ''kuni no miyatsuko'' only later, and that the ''Kojiki'''s account, which makes Kihisatsumi, the guardian of Kihisa rooted in the worship of Kamunabi-yama, their ancestor, preserves an older form of the Izumo ''kuni no miyatsuko'' tradition.{{Sfn|高嶋|1995a|pp=144-151}}

One reading holds that Kihisatsumi's decorating the green-leafed mountain to offer the great meal was Izumo's attempt to serve {{ill|Yamato kingship|ja|ヤマト王権|lt=Yamato|lt_ja=倭}} and improve relations between the two, but that it was interrupted because Homuchiwake spoke just before the offering, so that Izumo's submission to Yamato was never completed; layered with the later failure of the marriage between Homuchiwake and {{ill|Hinaga-hime|ja|ヒナガヒメ|lt=Hinaga-hime|lt_ja=ヒナガヒメ}}, this foreshadows Izumo becoming a target of conquest in the section on {{ill|Emperor Keikō|ja|景行天皇|lt=Emperor Keikō|lt_ja=景行天皇}}.{{Sfn|岡本|2007|pp=67-74}} It has also been argued that the offering was not submission but a rite for the "great god of Izumo", that Homuchiwake was a shaman possessed by the great god of Izumo, and that Kihisatsumi was the master of spirits who dealt with him.{{Sfn|アンダソヴァ|2012|pp=3-5}}

"The Sono-no-miya of Iwakuma in Izumo" has been identified with the Kizuki Taisha ({{ill|Izumo-taisha|ja|出雲大社|lt=Izumo-taisha|lt_ja=出雲大社}}),{{Sfn|尾崎|1966|pp=391-392}}{{Sfn|西郷|1988|p=252}} with the {{ill|Namesa Shrine|ja|那売佐神社|lt=Namesa Shrine|lt_ja=那売佐神社}} in {{ill|Kando District|ja|神門郡|lt=Kando District|lt_ja=神門郡}},{{Sfn|尾崎|1966|pp=391-392}} and with the Sokinoya shrine in Izumo District.{{Sfn|高嶋|1995a|pp=144-151}}{{Sfn|三谷|1974|pp=471-474}} The ''Izumo no Kuni Fudoki'' records that the shrine of Kihisakamitakahiko, who dwells at the Sokinoya shrine, stands on the peak of Kamunabi-yama.{{Sfn|中村|2015|pp=185, 271}}

Kihisatsumi is held to correspond to the 15th (or 14th) generation of the {{ill|Izumo kuni no miyatsuko|ja|出雲国造#系譜|lt=Izumo kuni no miyatsuko genealogy|lt_ja=出雲国造系図}}, written variously 来日曰維積命, 来日田維命, 来昌維績命, 来昌維命, 来日田准命, 来日田維穂命 and 来目田維穂命.{{Sfn|高嶋|1995a|pp=144-151}}{{Sfn|三谷|1974|pp=471-474}}{{Sfn|高嶋|1995b|pp=175-179}} Takashima Hiroshi takes the variant spellings to be the result of repeated copying errors, and supposes that the original spellings were 来日 for ''kihi'', 羅 for ''sa'' and 積 for ''tsumi'', so that the god's original name was {{lang|ja|来日羅積命}}.{{Sfn|高嶋|1995a|pp=144-151}} An example of reading 羅 as ''sa'' is poem 1159 of the ''{{ill|Man'yōshū|ja|万葉集|lt=Man'yōshū|lt_ja=万葉集}}'',{{efn|Its fifth line, 音之清羅, is read ''oto no sayakesa''.}} and 羅 is thought to have been used for the syllable ''sa'' because it has the same meaning as 紗, thin silk.{{Sfn|高嶋|1995a|pp=144-151}}{{Sfn|渡瀬|1985|pp=120-121}}
